items.title: New CFR Book by David Sacks Details the Life and Legacy of Hans Morgenthau
items.summary: “Americans owe it to themselves to take heed of Morgenthau’s sober vision of international politics. There is no better teacher of realism than Hans Morgenthau, the man who literally wrote the book on great-­power competition,” writes David Sacks, senior fellow for Asia studies at the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), in his new book, The Realist: […]

ai.sum: CFR published a book review of David Sacks' new book on Hans Morgenthau and realism.

brief.summary: The piece presents David Sacks's new CFR-published biography of Hans Morgenthau, founder of modern realism. It traces Morgenthau's path from Nazi-era Germany to exile in the United States and the writing of Politics Among Nations in 1948. The authors argue his thinking remains relevant to great-power competition, citing Russia's invasion of Ukraine and China's push to displace US influence. Sacks stresses that Morgenthau took ethics seriously, holding that norms restrain power but are only as strong as the power behind them. He also argues that Morgenthau saw the United States as exceptional, requiring its power to serve domestic democracy and liberty so it could serve as an example. The book uses research and interviews to examine Morgenthau's critique of the Vietnam War. The piece is a promotional and descriptive announcement rather than a policy paper.
brief.argument: Morgenthau's realist framework, with its sober view of power and its ethical limits, remains essential for understanding and navigating today's great-power competition.
recommendations: Americans should take heed of Morgenthau's sober vision of international politics.
US power should be married to purpose, serving democracy and liberty at home so the nation can set an example abroad.

items.title: Winning Time: Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces and the New Dimension of War
items.summary: In late 2023, Ukraine’s military leadership faced an institutional choice: establish a dedicated branch of the armed forces for unmanned systems or integrate drones into existing branches. Most senior officers I knew opposed the separate force, and their strongest argument was sound within classical doctrine. Each branch of service corresponds to a distinct domain of war: The army fights on land, the navy at sea, the air force in the air. Unmanned systems operate across all…

ai.sum: An analysis examines Ukraine's 2023 decision to create a dedicated Unmanned Systems Forces branch rather than integrate drones into existing services.

brief.summary: Oleksiy Honcharuk, a former Ukrainian prime minister who advised Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, argues that the war has opened a new contest he calls the Time Domain: a race over how quickly each side can adapt its tactics and technology. He contends that adaptation speed, not only mass or position, decides outcomes, and that Ukraine's drone units won by building the 'Combat Hub', a fused structure of combat, analytics, R&D and production. He presents the 412th Brigade 'Nemesis' and Lasar's Group as examples, and argues that a dedicated branch gives the contest an owner. He extends the case to deterrence, arguing that visible adaptation capacity can deter as stockpiles once did, while warning that a closing window can invite aggression. He ends by urging allies to build this capacity before the next war.
brief.argument: Adaptation speed is a distinct contest of war, the Time Domain, and the institution that wins it (the Combat Hub inside a dedicated branch) should be built in advance as a deterrent.
recommendations: Add a temporal axis to planning, tracking how long each side needs to move from identifying a tactic to fielding a countermeasure.
Procure adaptation cycles rather than fixed systems, favouring modular kit and contractual feedback between frontline operators and manufacturers.
Train for adaptability against opposition whose methods cannot be predicted, rather than rehearsing fixed scenarios.
Create a dedicated, bounded force or enclave with its own procurement rules, budget line and legal existence to pursue the contest.
brief.turkey: Türkiye's drone and defence-industry planners can draw on the argument that adaptation cycles, not inventories, should drive procurement and force structure, a point relevant to its own unmanned programmes and to how it reads Ukrainian and Russian drone innovation.

items.title: Europe Defense Dilemma | Council on Foreign Relations

ai.sum: A Council on Foreign Relations analysis examines the dilemmas facing European defence.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Europe must prepare for a future of limited or conditional U.S. support, with Russia remaining the main threat regardless of any Ukraine ceasefire. They set out three models: a more European NATO, in which Europeans take primary responsibility for conventional defence while the U.S. keeps nuclear guarantees; a European defence union built on the EU's mutual assistance and solidarity clauses; and a flexible coalition of willing European states including Ukraine. Each model carries different military, legal, industrial and transatlantic trade-offs. They conclude the likeliest outcome is a combination of all three, with a coalition offering political flexibility in crises but needing permanent NATO or EU support structures. The piece stresses investment, capability development and defence-industrial expansion as common priorities.
brief.argument: Europe will likely combine a reformed NATO, an EU defence union and an ad hoc coalition of willing states, because no single model can reliably deter Russia amid U.S. disengagement.
recommendations: Treat the three models as complementary rather than mutually exclusive.
Prioritise defence investment, capability development and defence-industrial expansion.
Build a durable coalition of willing European states, including Ukraine, backed by permanent NATO or EU structures.
Make EU Article 42(7) and 222 operational by adding response planning and lowering the Solidarity Clause threshold.
brief.turkey: A European defence coalition or EU defence union that excludes Türkiye would change the security architecture Ankara depends on through NATO, and any European defence-industrial autonomy could affect Turkish defence industry cooperation with European partners.

Now come claims in The Wall Street Journal about financial and political demands by the Houthis, which Ambassador Raed Qarmli, the Saudi Foreign Ministry’s Undersecretary for Public Diplomacy, categorically denied. ai.sum: Opinion piece argues Middle East reporting is becoming more misleading, citing disputed Wall Street Journal claims about Houthi demands.

brief.summary: The authors, writing in Al Majalla, argue that misleading Middle East reporting is increasing, pointing to a Reuters retraction over unverified explosion reports in Dubai and a Wall Street Journal story on Houthi demands that Saudi diplomat Raed Qarmli denied. They distinguish a retraction from a denial and identify three explanations for poor coverage. First, correspondents reporting from afar, relying on websites and social media, must compensate with a wider network of sources. Second, repeating one origin claim across many outlets can create the false impression of independent confirmation. Third, confirmation bias and simple inexperience lead to errors, such as treating an armed group's demands as legitimate while ignoring a recognised government. The argument is that audiences should scrutinise whose voices are included, excluded, or doubted.
brief.argument: Misleading Middle East reporting is rising because distant or inexperienced journalists rely on unverified social media, echo a single origin claim as if it were many sources, and let bias or weak regional understanding shape their coverage.
recommendations: Trace claims back to their original source before presenting them as exclusive information.
Compensate for distance by drawing on a broader network of vetted local contacts and sources.
Examine editorial choices, including whom reporters consult, exclude, or treat with suspicion, to detect confirmation bias.
Distinguish a militia's territorial control from any claim to represent the state, and account for internationally recognised governments.

Among the attractions is a celebrated mountain refuge, the Rifugio Guide del Cervino. Its name leaves little doubt about its origins. Built by Italians in 1984, it has welcomed visitors for four decades. Several years ago, its location became…

ai.sum: Article examines how climate change is reshaping national borders, using the Italy-Switzerland Alpine border as an example.

brief.summary: The authors argue that climate change is physically reshaping the geography on which international borders depend, so that legal boundaries built on natural features are becoming unstable. They use the Testa Grigia refuge, where glacier retreat moved a watershed boundary and left most of the building on Swiss territory, as an illustration. They say rivers that form borders are especially vulnerable, since climate-driven erosion, flooding and shifting channels can trigger disputes over sovereignty, water and hydropower. On the sea, they note that rising levels (about 20cm from 1901 to 2018, with more expected) and thermal expansion can push coastlines inland, threatening low-lying island states. Drawing on UNCLOS, they show that baselines, territorial seas, EEZs and continental shelves are all measured from the coastline, so shifts could shrink claimed maritime zones and access to hydrocarbons and fisheries. They frame the problem as a legal and economic risk that requires careful documentation of boundaries.
brief.argument: Climate-driven changes to rivers, glaciers and coastlines are altering the physical reference points on which legal borders and maritime entitlements rest, creating new sovereignty, resource and legal disputes.
recommendations: Legally secure maritime boundaries and document their geographical coordinates.
Reach international understandings that prevent climate change from becoming a pretext for territorial or resource disputes.
Negotiate boundary adjustments, as Italy and Switzerland have done over the Testa Grigia refuge.

items.summary: A year before the largest cryptocurrency theft in history, students at an Atlantic Council cyber strategy competition encountered an eerily similar scenario. The post What students got right about the $6 billion Binance hack, and how they would prevent the next one appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council reports that students at a cyber strategy competition anticipated a scenario resembling the $6 billion Binance hack.

brief.summary: The authors compare the October 2026 Binance hack, attributed to North Korea's TraderTraitor group, with a fictional scenario that university students worked through in the Atlantic Council's Cyber 9/12 Strategy Challenge the previous November. They find the students' proposals anticipated several real responses: rapid freezing of stolen funds, cautious but eventually confident attribution, and sanctions aimed at cash-out networks rather than only the hackers. They argue the students also missed two things. First, the real exchange absorbed the losses itself, which raises unresolved questions about who bears the cost of major thefts. Second, the attackers targeted employees through social engineering, while the students' fixes focused mainly on wallet custody. The piece presents the exercise as a way to find policy gaps before a real crisis.
brief.argument: Student crisis-response proposals anticipated much of the real Binance response but overlooked liability for losses and the human targeting of exchange staff, gaps that exercises like Cyber 9/12 can surface before the next heist.
recommendations: Formalise rapid freezing of stolen funds through a standing network of exchanges, analytics firms, financial intelligence units and stablecoin issuers rather than relying on goodwill.
Attribute publicly once evidence is strong, since delay can cost time needed for freezes and sanctions.
Target the wallets and intermediaries that convert crypto to cash, not only the hackers.
Build expedited mutual legal assistance channels with Southeast Asian partners such as ASEAN before stolen funds move.

(Getty Images) Toggle Table of Contents Contents…

ai.sum: Hudson Institute authors argue that the transatlantic alliance needs a capital pillar.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the transatlantic alliance needs a third pillar beside military deterrence: control over capital. They contend Europe screens who owns its strategic assets but not who finances them, and that Chinese state-backed credit, buyer's credit, vendor finance and bundled construction contracts can create control that equity screening misses. They also argue that de-risking from China is an unfunded capital problem, since replacing vendors and restructuring supply chains require financing that banks, institutional investors, national public lenders and private capital each struggle to supply alone. Their proposed answer is a strategic capital facility with four eligibility tests (origin of funds, terms, embedded control, substitutability), a replacement window for excluded infrastructure, a European guarantee counterpart, and mobilisation of regional private investors, with US participation via the DFC.
brief.argument: Europe must extend its security screening to the origin and terms of financing and build a publicly backed, transatlantic capital facility so that rejecting risky Chinese finance is economically feasible.
recommendations: Extend EU investment screening to credit and quasi-credit exposures on critical infrastructure above a threshold, including vendor finance, leasing and bundled EPC packages.
Create a transatlantic strategic capital facility with EU and member-state first-loss protection, EIB/EBRD credit enhancement, and DFC participation, with private investors providing senior capital.
Establish a dedicated financing window for removing and replacing excluded high-risk vendor equipment in networks.
Consolidate or interoperate national export credit and political risk insurance agencies across member states.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Serbia's new Student List government, which took office after the October 2026 election, should not let its September commitment to join the Vertical Gas Corridor lapse. brief.argument: Belgrade's new government should keep the Vertical Gas Corridor commitment on track because it diversifies Serbia's gas supply and advances the Student List's own transparency, economic and investment goals without forcing a Brussels-or-Moscow choice.
recommendations: Keep the Vertical Gas Corridor commitment on track through the government transition

brief.summary: The authors argue that elections rarely produce major foreign policy change, and that the high-profile 2026 votes are unlikely to be the exception. They offer two explanations: voters usually rank foreign policy below economic and social concerns, and states have fairly fixed interests and entrenched alliances and rivalries that make sharp reversals costly and slow. Governments therefore tend to adjust existing approaches rather than transform them, and they put their new mandates into domestic agendas. They note that opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot criticised the war on Iran but still backs action against its nuclear programme, and that his Palestine plan would not greatly differ from Netanyahu's.
brief.argument: Electoral change usually yields only nuanced foreign policy adjustments, because voters prioritise domestic issues and states' interests and alliances are structurally fixed.

They add that the Bush administration's distraction with Iraq left the early Taliban resurgence unaddressed, and that Washington never pressed Pakistan hard enough over its sanctuaries and support for the Taliban and Haqqani network. The surge into Marjah and Helmand, rather than securing Kabul and Kandahar, squandered momentum, and firing McChrystal weakened it further. Finally, they argue the US missed a cheaper option in 2017: using money and contractors to rent the loyalty of regional power-brokers, as Najibullah had done.
brief.argument: The US lost in Afghanistan because of six avoidable strategic choices, chiefly the attempt to build a centralised state and the failure to pressure Pakistan, rather than because the war was unwinnable.

Match force posture to the political goals set, rather than pursuing a light footprint alongside ambitious nation-building

brief.summary: The authors argue that the autumn and winter mud season known as rasputitsa will constrain Russian mechanised manoeuvre in Ukraine, since saturated ground slows tracked and wheeled vehicles, forces artillery onto roads and raises fuel use and breakdowns. They show that the same seasonal pattern has recurred across four years of war and that the 2022 advance on Kyiv was hampered by it. They then turn to Russia's rear support: the occupied Ukrainian rail network is damaged, Russia has built new Sea of Azov lines at high cost, and freeze-thaw cycles, erosion and poor maintenance strain these tracks. Freight and revenue figures for the Novorossiya Railways show declines. The authors expect Russia to lean more on drone and missile strikes, and see little prospect that trilateral negotiations will produce a settlement.
brief.argument: The coming rasputitsa will constrain Russian battlefield manoeuvre and strain its already fragile railway supply network in occupied Ukraine, pushing Moscow toward greater reliance on long-range strikes rather than producing a diplomatic breakthrough.
brief.turkey: Seasonal ground and rail constraints on Russian logistics in Ukraine bear on Black Sea and Azov dynamics that matter to Türkiye's security calculus, though the piece does not address Türkiye directly.

items.title: Die Integration der CO2-Entnahme in den Emissionshandel der EU
items.summary: Für den technologischen Hochlauf bietet der Kommissionsvorschlag zu wenig Anreize

ai.sum: SWP analysis argues the Commission's proposal offers too few incentives for integrating CO2 removal into the EU emissions trading system.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Commission's July 2026 ETS reform, which would auction 250 million extra allowances from 2031 to 2040 to buy permanent EU carbon removals (BioCCS and DACCS), creates the first EU-policy-driven demand for removals but gives too few and too late incentives. Revenue depends on uncertain carbon prices and removal costs, which the impact assessment assumes will fall by 2030 without evidence, and payment-on-delivery sits poorly with capital-intensive projects. The paper warns that a shortfall could push policy toward cheaper methods such as biochar or land-based removals, and toward international credits. Both options risk weakening the LULUCF target and shifting emissions abroad. The authors call for supply-side support and funding instruments to be settled during the negotiations rather than deferred.
brief.argument: The Commission's ETS removal proposal creates demand but lacks the revenue certainty and supply-side support needed to deliver removals at scale, and opening it to cheaper methods would undermine integrity and the LULUCF target.
recommendations: Decide during the ongoing negotiations which instruments will fund the gap between removal costs and ETS revenues.
Add supply-side support such as public procurement, capacity-building subsidies or carbon contracts for difference alongside the ETS demand signal.
Keep the eligible methods limited to durable geological removals to protect integrity, and avoid shifting biomass into the ETS.
Strengthen the forest and land sink through measures such as less harvesting and peatland rewetting rather than relying on ETS-funded removals.

items.title: Putin suffers Balkan setbacks as Russia struggles to retain influence
items.summary: Russia’s recent setbacks in the Balkans are a reminder of the foreign policy challenges facing the Kremlin as the full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches a sixth year with no end in sight, writes Michael Getto. The post Putin suffers Balkan setbacks as Russia struggles to retain influence appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council analysis says recent Russian setbacks in the Balkans show Moscow struggling to retain influence as the Ukraine war nears its fifth year.

brief.summary: The author argues that a run of political changes has left Russia on the defensive across several regions. A student-led movement ousted Serbia's long-serving President Vucic in a late-October vote, removing a consistently pro-Russian voice in Europe. In Romania, a new pro-EU government ended a five-month deadlock after Bucharest shot down Russian drones over the Black Sea, and the author sees this as providing stability and likely firmer backing for Ukraine. Hungary's Orban, widely seen as Moscow's unofficial representative inside NATO and the EU, lost power in April, and his successor is described as more pragmatic toward Kyiv and firmer on Russia. The piece adds setbacks in Venezuela, Syria and the South Caucasus, while noting Russia's ties with China, Iran and North Korea remain strong and that it is too early to write off Putin.
brief.argument: Recent electoral and geopolitical setbacks in the Balkans, Central Europe and beyond are eroding Russia's influence, though Moscow retains significant partners and room to recover.

items.title: Last week’s brief Ukraine ceasefire did not stop Russian attacks on civilians
items.summary: A recent humanitarian ceasefire around the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky made it possible to evacuate hundreds of residents, but Russian attacks on civilians elsewhere in Ukraine continue, writes Kristina Hook. The post Last week’s brief Ukraine ceasefire did not stop Russian attacks on civilians appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: A brief humanitarian ceasefire around Oleshky allowed evacuation of civilians, but Russian attacks on civilians elsewhere in Ukraine continued.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the brief, localised Oleshky ceasefire, which allowed hundreds of civilians to leave Russian-occupied Oleshky, was a real humanitarian success but should not be read as a shift in Moscow's position. They say the evacuation must not obscure what made it necessary: Russian occupation, the 2023 Kakhovka dam destruction, and mining that emptied a city of about 24,000 people to under 2,000. They contend that staged cooperation, such as Ukrainian and Russian officials thanking each other, reflects Kyiv's wish to save lives rather than trust in the performance, and that the Russian ombudswoman involved is accused of facilitating child deportations. They note that Russian strikes on civilians continued during the pause, including a deadly attack on a school aid point in Zaporizhzhia the day after it ended. The authors call for scrutiny of humanitarian pauses and for continued independent monitoring and accountability.
brief.argument: The Oleshky ceasefire saved lives but does not signal any broader Russian willingness to stop attacking Ukrainian civilians or end the invasion.
recommendations: Keep independent monitoring and accountability in focus after humanitarian pauses end
Do not treat localised, staged cooperation as evidence of a change in Russian policy
Use precise language that attributes responsibility for civilian suffering to Russia

The author expects Congress to press for tougher China policy, support Taiwan arms sales, and curb tariffs, which Asian officials see as unpopular with Americans. However, the author warns that a lame-duck Trump, isolated from advisers, could be unpredictable and might resume attacks on Iran, which would hurt US standing in Asia. brief.argument: Asian allies hope the post-midterm Congress will push US foreign policy, especially on Iran, but these hopes cannot be taken for granted given Trump's unpredictability.

items.title: COP31 in Turkey: What to Expect
items.summary: The 2026 UN climate summit faces mounting pressure to accelerate climate action and deliver on implementation, as projections indicate that the world will overshoot the 1.5°C (2.7°F) global warming threshold, raising questions about the legacy of the Paris Agreement.

ai.sum: Türkiye will host COP31 in 2026, with the summit facing pressure to accelerate climate action as the 1.5°C threshold looks likely to be overshot.

brief.summary: The authors preview COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye (9–20 November), which falls on the tenth anniversary of the Paris Agreement's entry into force and proceeds without an official US delegation. They argue that the summit's new COP31 presidency is pushing from pledges toward implementation, with an Action Agenda and voluntary pledges on electrification and sustainable AI. They note real progress, with projected warming down to about 2.8°C under current policies, but judge the 1.5°C goal out of reach. They identify finance, fossil fuel language, emissions reductions, adaptation metrics and a just transition mechanism as the main contested issues. They also flag headwinds such as delays in IPCC reporting and shifting national politics. Their conclusion is that COP31 will likely produce no single breakthrough, though its value lies in keeping climate on the global agenda and building coalitions, notably on methane.
brief.argument: COP31 is unlikely to yield a major breakthrough, and its value lies mainly in sustaining implementation pressure and coalition-building on climate action.
recommendations: Developed countries should deliver on existing climate finance commitments, including the goal of $300 billion per year by 2035.
Countries should accelerate methane emissions cuts, particularly in the oil and gas sectors, where low-cost options exist.
Parties should resolve the timeline for the next IPCC reports so that national commitments rest on current science.
brief.turkey: Türkiye hosts COP31 as president, and the authors' framing of implementation as the test of the summit places Ankara's presidency under scrutiny for delivering concrete outcomes.

items.summary: Conversations with several Sadrists reveal a movement preparing to fill a leadership vacuum in Iraq—and engage with the US. The post Washington should broaden its Shia outreach in Iraq. Muqtada al-Sadr is a case study. appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: An Atlantic Council analysis argues Washington should broaden its outreach to Iraqi Shia actors, using Muqtada al-Sadr's movement as a case study.

brief.summary: The authors read Muqtada al-Sadr's October 2026 post addressed to Washington as a signal that he is repositioning as a nationalist, more open-to-the-US Shia alternative to the Coordination Framework. Drawing on conversations with Sadrists, they describe the movement preparing to return to power as the Framework's rule weakens under economic strain, with Iraq's oil revenue losses after the Hormuz closure and the stalled militia disarmament plan adding pressure. They identify two obstacles to his rise: eroded cohesion inside the Sadrist movement after years of withdrawal, and opposition from the Najaf clerical establishment that prefers multiple Shia factions in power. They conclude that Washington should stop treating Iraq's Shia as a reflection of Iran and widen its engagement with non-Iran-aligned Shia voices, with Gulf allies encouraged to do the same.
brief.argument: Al-Sadr is positioning himself as a viable, US-friendly Shia alternative to Iran-aligned ruling parties, and Washington should broaden its engagement with non-Iranian Shia voices in Iraq.
recommendations: Broaden engagement with the range of Shia voices in Iraq rather than treating the community as an extension of the Iranian regime
Encourage Gulf allies, who are closer to Iraqi Shia culturally and linguistically, to engage similarly

ai.sum: Hudson Institute analysts Tsiporah Fried and Luke Coffey argue the 2026 US midterm results are more complex than a simple Democratic wave.

brief.summary: The authors, two Hudson Institute analysts, argue that the November 2026 midterms were a vote of censure against Donald Trump rather than an endorsement of a Democratic platform. Voters judged his record against his promises, with cost of living as the leading concern, followed by anger over the Iran war, the handling of immigration enforcement, and perceived corruption. They describe the result as a real Democratic gain, including flips in conservative states, but caution that the Democratic coalition is held together more by opposition to Trump than by a shared agenda, and that its factions (progressive, pragmatic moderate, establishment) remain divided. On the Republican side they map competing currents (isolationists, prioritizers, Reaganites, nationalists) and argue the party brand has been punished, with succession to 2028 wide open. They read J.D. Vance's distancing from the president as constrained by his position, and see Marco Rubio's next moves as a test of how much he separates from the MAGA agenda. They close by urging France to abandon ideological readings of American politics.
brief.argument: The midterms were a rebuke of Trump's broken promises rather than a shift to a coherent Democratic ideology, and the post-Trump succession on both sides remains unsettled.

items.title: A Green Electrification Target for All?
items.summary: COP31 as a Catalyst for European Clean-Tech Diplomacy

ai.sum: A SWP analysis discusses COP31 as a catalyst for European clean-tech diplomacy and electrification targets.

brief.summary: The authors examine the proposed global electrification target for COP31, hosted by Türkiye and Australia in Antalya, which would raise electricity's share of global energy consumption from 20 to 35 per cent by 2035. They note the target is non-binding and not restricted to green sources, which puts it partly at odds with the fossil-fuel phase-out process launched by Brazil. Electrification is presented as a complement to the green energy transition that also serves energy security and competitiveness, especially after recent oil and gas price shocks. The authors describe a balancing act for the EU between cooperating with China, which dominates clean-tech supply, and protecting European producers. They judge agreement at Antalya uncertain, given developing countries' demands for finance, and argue Germany and the EU should pursue bilateral clean-tech cooperation beyond COP31 through initiatives such as Electrify Now.
brief.argument: A green electrification target can advance climate, energy security and competitiveness, but its success at COP31 depends on finance for developing countries and on Europe balancing cooperation with China against protecting its clean-tech industry.
recommendations: Explicitly name green electrification as a strategic goal in Germany and the EU.
Restrict the global electrification target to renewable electricity sources and make it monitorable through NDCs.
Use the Electrify Now initiative as a platform to engage middle powers and trading partners on clean-tech cooperation.
Advance bilateral clean-tech diplomacy to secure markets in third countries and support European producers against Chinese competition.
brief.turkey: As COP31 host, Türkiye is pushing a non-binding electrification pledge whose success will depend on diplomatic skill and credible financial incentives for developing countries.

They say this has fuelled Algerian anxiety, prompting Algiers to re-engage in the Sahel, normalise ties with Mali, and cut relations with the UAE. The piece concludes that by choosing a side, Washington may have made regional peace less likely, even as it claims to want to end the frozen conflict.
brief.argument: US backing of Morocco's Western Sahara plan is incompatible with its stated goal of brokering peace and is deepening zero-sum rivalry in North Africa and the Sahel.
